title: Thompson v. North American Stainless, LP (2011)
shortTitle: Thompson v. North American Stainless, LP — zone-of-interests note
summary: An employee fired in retaliation for his fiancee's discrimination charge is a person aggrieved under Title VII because he falls within the zone of interests the statute protects.
notes:
Key line: "Applying that test here, we conclude that Thompson falls within the zone of interests protected by Title VII." Justice Scalia, for the Court.

Citation: 562 U.S. 170 (2011).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was Eric L. Thompson, an employee of North American Stainless in Kentucky. Respondent was North American Stainless, LP, a steel company that employed both Thompson and his fiancee, Miriam Regalado. Regalado had filed a sex discrimination charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Thompson claimed that the company fired him to punish Regalado for her charge. The company argued that Thompson had engaged in no protected activity of his own and therefore was not within the class of persons Title VII allows to sue.
sections.Material Facts: Until 2003 both Thompson and Regalado worked for North American Stainless. In February 2003 the EEOC notified the company that Regalado had filed a charge alleging sex discrimination. Three weeks later the company fired Thompson. Thompson filed his own charge with the EEOC, and after conciliation failed he sued under Title VII, alleging that the company fired him in order to retaliate against Regalado. Title VII's antiretaliation provision, 42 U.S.C. 2000e-3(a), makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against any of his employees because he has made a charge. Section 2000e-5(f)(1) permits a civil action by a person claiming to be aggrieved. For purposes of the appeal the courts assumed that the company fired Thompson to retaliate against Regalado.
sections.Procedural History: Thompson sued in the Eastern District of Kentucky, which granted summary judgment to the company on the ground that Title VII does not permit third-party retaliation claims. A Sixth Circuit panel reversed, but the en banc court granted rehearing and affirmed the District Court by a vote of 10 to 6 in 2009, reasoning that Thompson had engaged in no protected activity and was not within the class Congress protected. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on December 7, 2010, and on January 24, 2011 reversed and remanded.
sections.Issue: Title VII forbids an employer to discriminate against any of his employees because he has made a charge of discrimination, and it permits a civil action by a person claiming to be aggrieved. Thompson filed no charge of his own; the company allegedly fired him to punish his fiancee for her charge. Did firing Thompson to retaliate against his fiancee constitute unlawful retaliation under Title VII, and if so, does the statute give Thompson, who engaged in no protected activity himself, a cause of action as a person claiming to be aggrieved by the unlawful employment practice?
sections.Holding: Yes on both questions. Under Burlington Northern v. White, the antiretaliation provision reaches any employer action that might dissuade a reasonable worker from making a charge, and a reasonable worker would be dissuaded if she knew her fiance would be fired. Thompson is a person aggrieved because that term incorporates the zone-of-interests test, and as an employee who was the intended means of harming Regalado, he falls within the zone of interests Title VII protects. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Scalia first held that the firing violated Title VII. Burlington construed the antiretaliation provision broadly to cover conduct that would deter protected activity, and firing a fiance obviously would. The Court acknowledged that third-party reprisals create line-drawing problems about which relationships are protected but declined to adopt a fixed rule, saying that firing a close family member will almost always qualify while milder reprisals against acquaintances almost never will. On the cause of action, the Court rejected two extremes. Reading aggrieved to reach anyone with Article III standing would produce absurd results, such as allowing a shareholder to sue over a company's firing of a valuable employee. Reading it to cover only the employee who engaged in protected activity would be artificially narrow, since the term aggrieved is broader than that. The Court adopted a middle position, borrowing the zone-of-interests test from APA cases: a person aggrieved is one with an interest arguably sought to be protected by the statute. Thompson was an employee of the company, and Title VII exists to protect employees from their employers' unlawful acts. He was not collateral damage but the intended instrument of the retaliation, so hurting him was the unlawful act by which the employer punished Regalado. He therefore could sue.

topics.lrs-n-standing-zone: Intentional retaliatory targeting placed the employee within the statute’s interests.
topics.lrs-n-standing-apa702: Thompson reads Title VII's 'person aggrieved' by reference to the APA § 702 zone-of-interests test.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 8 to 0. Justice Ginsburg concurred, joined by Justice Breyer, noting that the EEOC's Compliance Manual had long recognized that Title VII prohibits retaliation against someone closely related to or associated with the person who engaged in protected activity. Justice Kagan took no part.
